title: a rich kid who saw a sick man, an old man, a corpse, and a monk
hook: a rich kid who saw a sick man, an old man, a corpse, and a monk

segments.voice: Yesterday: dukkha, the wobble in the wheel. Your line was this too. Did something small go wrong, and did the words help? Day four.

A prince grows up in the foothills of the Himalayas. His father has given him everything. Palaces, music, fine clothes, and, the story says, a life kept carefully away from anything ugly. Then one day he goes out riding. By the road he sees an old man, bent over. Then a sick man. Then a dead body being carried to the fire. Then a wandering monk, owning nothing, and somehow calm. Four sights. He goes home and can't stop thinking about them. That rich kid is the person the whole path is named after.
screen: `A PRINCE WHO HAD EVERYTHING.` → `FOUR SIGHTS BY THE ROAD.` → `HE CAN'T STOP THINKING.`

segments.voice: Buddha isn't a name. It's a title. It comes from a Pali and Sanskrit root, budh, to wake up. A buddha is someone who has woken up. Tradition gives his name as Siddhattha, of the Gotama family, from the Sakya people, in the borderlands of what's now Nepal and India. Scholars still argue about exactly when he lived. The four sights you just heard are how later tellings of his life begin, and that's worth being honest about. In the early discourses, a very similar story is told about an earlier buddha, and the Buddha himself remembers his young life more plainly: a sheltered, comfortable home, and a growing shock at aging, sickness and death. The four sights may be a story. The question inside them is real. Here's what that rich kid did with it, as tradition tells it. He left the palace, lived for years as a wandering seeker, nearly starved himself, gave that up, sat down under a tree, and woke up. Then he spent the rest of his life walking the roads of northern India, teaching kings and farmers, women and men. And here's a surprise. In one discourse, a man named Dona sees his footprints, follows them, and asks: are you a god? No, he says. A heavenly musician? A spirit? No. A human being? No, again. Then what are you? Remember me, he says, as awake: a buddha. He was born a person, the story agrees. What he says he became is awake. Theravada teaching stresses that he was a human being who found a way and showed it. Mahayana traditions also speak of buddhas on a vast, cosmic scale. Both tell the story starting with a person.
screen: `BUDDHA — ONE WHO WOKE UP.` · `SIDDHATTHA GOTAMA, OF THE SAKYAS.` · `THE PALACE, THE ROAD, THE TREE.` · `NOT A GOD. AWAKE.` · then, large: `HE WAS A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of an old face you know. On the second, think of someone who is sick, or has been. On the third, think of the calmest person you've ever met. Three of the four sights he saw are close to anyone, any day. For three breaths, let yourself see them.
The Buddha. Not a name but a title: the one who woke up. A person who found a way, and spent his life showing it. Fourth word.
Your line: he was a person. Today, look at one statue, picture or image of the Buddha you pass, on a shelf, in a shop, online, and remember the story: it starts with a person. Day four.

howItsDone: Buddhists honor the Buddha as a teacher and example, bowing to his image, offering flowers, light and incense at shrines, and celebrating his birth, awakening and death, which Theravada Buddhists mark together on the festival of Vesak.

myth: it's a title: the one who woke up. his name was Siddhattha Gotama.
asked if he was a god, the Buddha said yes
asked if he was a god, a spirit or even a human, he said no each time: remember me as awake.
the early discourses tell a four-sights story about an earlier buddha
a very similar story is told of Vipassi, a buddha long before him.

fork.setup: someone meets the Buddha on the road and asks: are you a god? a spirit? a man? what does he answer, in the story?
fork.reveal: he answers that he is awake: a buddha. not a claim to godhood, and not quite 'just a man' either. a person who woke up.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakened, from the root budh, to wake up.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha is the god of Buddhism.
what it means: a title, the awakened one, for a man named Siddhattha Gotama who found a way and spent the rest of his life teaching it.
what a scholar hears: buddha, past participle of budh. the four-sights story comes from later biographies; in the Digha Nikaya (DN 14) a similar story is told of an earlier buddha, Vipassi.

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the four sights told of the earlier buddha Vipassi
Sukhamala Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.38): his own memory of a sheltered youth
